anomaly_def.Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statement or transaction design forces the engine to process far more data or rows than the true business need. 
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database-related processes saturate host CPU cycles, creating system-wide compute contention. 
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced limits on file handles, threads, shared memory, or similar objects are reached, preventing the database from acquiring additional OS resources. 

When all three root causes coexist, the database exhibits a layered failure pattern: statement latencies grow long and variable; CPU utilization hovers at or above core capacity with high run-queue lengths; meanwhile, new sessions, parallel workers, or I/O requests intermittently fail with "too many open files," "cannot create thread," or shared-memory errors. Slow-query logs and performance views show repeated, bloated SQL with extreme CPU time, while the error log and system journal simultaneously record kernel resource-limit denials. End-user symptoms range from sporadic timeouts and retries to partial outages where existing sessions crawl while new connections are rejected.

Causally, inefficient SQL constructs (wide scans, Cartesian joins, long-lived transactions) drive excessive CPU demand. The resulting saturation lengthens task runtimes and escalates context switches, increasing the number of concurrent threads, open file descriptors, and asynchronous I/O contexts the database tries to allocate. As CPU pressure rises, the engine spawns more background or parallel workers in an attempt to keep up, rapidly depleting kernel-level quotas. Once an OS limit is hit, the database cannot create additional execution or I/O resources, which forces even well-written queries to queue behind stuck tasks, further extending transaction lifetimes and compounding CPU consumption. The feedback loop—inefficient SQL → CPU exhaustion → kernel limit exhaustion → wider systemic slowdown—amplifies each individual anomaly and can culminate in cascading service degradation or outage.

entry.official_definition: Specifies the timeout in seconds for attempts to acquire metadata locks.
entry.trigger_condition: A statement waits longer than lock_wait_timeout while attempting to acquire a metadata lock.
entry.workload_impact: The metadata lock acquisition fails and the statement does not proceed.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as a MySQL server system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when a statement cannot obtain the required lock within the configured waiting window because another transaction or metadata operation is holding an incompatible lock.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect blocking sessions, reduce conflicting transaction overlap, shorten transaction lifetime, and review lock scheduling and schema-change timing.
